questions.question: A routing table holds 500,000 card-number prefixes of up to eight digits. Roughly how does the cost of one trie lookup scale?
options: With the number of stored prefixes, about log2(500000) comparisons
With the length of the query, at most eight child-pointer steps regardless of table size
With both: the walk is eight steps, each of which binary-searches the stored prefixes
With the alphabet size, since every node must be scanned for the matching digit
questions.explanation: A trie walks one node per character of the query, so an eight-digit prefix is found in at most eight steps whether the table holds 50 or 500,000 entries. A balanced BST or sorted array would need about 19 comparisons. Child lookup inside a node is a map or array access, not a scan of the whole table.

questions.question: The trie stores the keys 4, 4111, and 51. What does longestPrefixMatch("411") return?
options: ("4111", ...) because 411 is a prefix of the stored key 4111
null, because 411 is a path in the trie but not a stored key
("4", ...) because 4 is the deepest terminal node on the path to 411
("411", ...) because the walk reaches a node spelling 411
questions.explanation: Longest-prefix match returns the longest stored key that is a prefix of the query, not the other way round. On the path 4 -> 41 -> 411 only the node for 4 is terminal, so ("4", ...) is returned. The node for 411 exists but is not terminal, and 4111 is longer than the query, so it cannot be a prefix of it.

questions.question: Keys 4111, 411, and 4 are stored on one path of five nodes. After delete("4111") and then delete("4"), how many nodes remain and which keys are still found?
options: 3 nodes; only 411 is found, because deleting 4 also pruned its subtree
4 nodes; only 411 is found, because the 4111 leaf was pruned and the 4 node stayed as a path
5 nodes; 411 and 4 are found, because delete only unmarks and never removes nodes
2 nodes; nothing is found, because deleting an ancestor key removes every descendant key
questions.explanation: Deleting 4111 unmarks its node, which now has no children and is not terminal, so it is pruned (5 -> 4 nodes); pruning stops at 411 because it is terminal. Deleting 4 unmarks that node but it still has a child, so nothing is removed and 411 remains reachable. A trie never deletes descendants when an ancestor key is removed.

questions.question: Why does rangeToPrefixes("2221", "2720") produce 23 prefixes rather than 500 four-digit keys?
options: Because any block of numbers that starts on a trailing-zero boundary and fits inside the range is covered by one shorter prefix, such as 23 for 2300-2399
Because the trie merges single-child chains automatically, collapsing 2300 through 2399 into one node after insertion
Because card numbers only use the digits 2 through 7 in those positions, so most four-digit combinations never occur
Because the algorithm rounds the range outward to the nearest hundreds, trading exactness for a smaller table
questions.explanation: The greedy decomposition widens a block while its start ends in zeros and its last number stays within hi: 2300-2399 is exactly the prefix 23. The result covers the range exactly, verified by the test over 2000-2999. The plain trie does not merge chains (that is a radix tree), and no rounding takes place.

questions.question: A processor's router uses a six-digit hash map and, on a miss, retries with five, four, three, two, then one digit. Which failure does a trie with longest-prefix match remove?
options: The hash map cannot store the two-digit Amex prefixes 34 and 37, because every key in it has to be padded to exactly six digits
Hash lookups are slower than trie walks for keys longer than four characters, so six attempts cost far more than one eight-step walk
The retry loop cannot handle 15-digit Amex PANs, because it assumes a 16-digit input when it slices off the leading six digits
A stale short rule such as 27 can win before the correct 2720 rule is ever checked, and every range must be expanded into tens of thousands of six-digit keys
questions.explanation: The retry loop encodes 'longest wins' by hand and is only as correct as the order and completeness of its six tables; a leftover 27 rule wins over 2720 if the four-digit table was never consulted first, and every range has to be expanded to the fixed key length. A trie stores each rule at its natural length and one walk returns the deepest match. Hash maps can hold short keys fine, and lookup speed is not the issue.

questions.question: The router's error message for an unroutable PAN prints 272100******0008 rather than the full number. Why is that a correctness requirement and not just a style choice?
options: Because the full PAN would push the exception message past the 80-character limit that most logging frameworks truncate at
Because the trailing digits are not part of the BIN and are therefore irrelevant to the routing decision
Because masking makes the message identical for every card in a BIN, which lets log aggregation group the errors
Because exception messages end up in logs, and PCI DSS forbids storing a full PAN anywhere but a protected cardholder-data store
questions.explanation: PCI DSS requirement 3 limits display and storage of the PAN to the first six and last four digits outside of protected systems, and a log line is storage. An exception message that includes the full PAN turns every log aggregator into cardholder data. The other options describe side effects, not the requirement.
